questions.question: What is Artificial Intelligence (AI)?

options.text: A database management system
A field evolved since the 1950s that makes machines perform tasks requiring human intelligence
A programming language for data analysis
A cloud storage service

explanation.correct: AI is an umbrella term for a field that has evolved since the 1950s, encompassing strategies and techniques for making machines perform tasks that typically require human intelligence.
explanation.why: A is a database tool, C is wrong category, D is storage — none capture the broad definition of AI.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT typically considered an example of AI?

options.text: Computer vision
Smart devices
Relational databases
Machine learning

explanation.correct: Relational databases are traditional data storage systems, not AI. Computer vision, smart devices, and ML are all examples of AI applications.
explanation.why: Relational databases use structured query logic, not intelligence or pattern learning.

questions.question: How is Machine Learning (ML) related to AI?

options.text: ML is a superset of AI
ML is completely separate from AI
ML is a subset of AI
ML replaced AI in 2020

explanation.correct: ML is a subset of AI. AI is the broad umbrella term, and ML is one group of techniques within it.
explanation.why: A is backwards — AI is the broader field. B and D are incorrect.

questions.question: What does an ML model do during the inference phase?

options.text: It downloads more training data
It applies what it learned during training to new input data to produce output
It deletes old parameters
It rewrites its own code

explanation.correct: Inference is the output the model produces by applying what it has learned during training to new input data.
explanation.why: A, C, D are all incorrect — inference is about applying a trained model, not modifying it.

questions.question: What is a 'prompt' in the context of generative AI?

options.text: A type of training dataset
An instruction or question in natural language that requests the model to perform a task
A hardware component for AI
A security policy for AI systems

explanation.correct: A prompt is an instruction or question written in natural language text that requests the generative AI model to perform a specific task.
explanation.why: A, C, D are unrelated to the definition of a prompt.

questions.question: What does LLM stand for?

options.text: Low-Level Machine
Large Language Model
Logical Learning Module
Linked Library Method

explanation.correct: LLM stands for Large Language Model — a foundation model pre-trained on massive amounts of text.
explanation.why: The other options are not real AI terminology.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes what an LLM is trained on?

options.text: Images and videos only
Audio recordings
Massive amounts of text — trillions of words
Structured database records

explanation.correct: LLMs are pre-trained extensively on massive amounts of text — trillions of words — which is why they excel at language tasks.
explanation.why: A, B, D are not the primary training data for LLMs.

questions.question: According to responsible AI principles, which three properties must an AI system maintain?

options.text: Fast, cheap, and scalable
Accurate/fair/safe, explainable/transparent, governed/controlled
Open-source, cloud-based, and multilingual
Automated, serverless, and encrypted

explanation.correct: Responsible AI practices require systems to be accurate/fair/safe/secure, explainable/transparent, and governed/controlled.
explanation.why: A, C, D describe infrastructure or business concerns, not core responsible AI principles.

questions.question: When should you choose traditional data analytics OVER machine learning?

options.text: When you have billions of unlabeled data points
When business rules can be hardcoded and variables are limited
When you need image recognition
When human language understanding is required

explanation.correct: Traditional analytics is appropriate when business rules can be hardcoded, variables are limited, statistical modeling works, and analytics can answer quickly enough.
explanation.why: A, C, D all suggest complex pattern recognition where ML is the better choice.

questions.question: What is the role of training data in an ML model?

options.text: It defines the infrastructure where the model runs
It is used to teach the model to recognize patterns so it can make predictions on new data
It is the output produced by the model
It stores the results of inference calls

explanation.correct: Training data is used to train the mathematical model so it learns to recognize patterns and can make accurate predictions when faced with new input.
explanation.why: A is infrastructure, C and D describe outputs, not training data.

questions.question: A law firm uses an AI tool to research case precedents. The tool generates citations that turn out to be completely fabricated. What type of AI problem is this?

options.text: Model overfitting
Hallucination — the model generating plausible but false information
Data poisoning
Bias in training data

explanation.correct: When AI models generate confident-sounding but false information (like fake citations), this is called hallucination — a known failure mode of generative AI.
explanation.why: Overfitting, data poisoning, and bias are related but different issues. Fabricated factual claims are specifically hallucinations.

questions.question: Which criterion for choosing ML is MOST important to assess first?

options.text: Whether the CEO mandated AI adoption
Whether you have enough relevant, high-quality training data
Whether a competitor is using ML
Whether the team can write Python

explanation.correct: Having enough relevant, high-quality training data is the foundational criterion. Without it, no ML approach will produce reliable results.
explanation.why: Mandates and competitive pressure don't determine ML success. Python is one tool among many.

questions.question: What does 'explainability' mean in responsible AI?

options.text: The model can explain jokes
Stakeholders can validate and understand what is happening inside the AI system
The code is open source
The model runs without human oversight

explanation.correct: Explainability means providing mechanisms to validate and audit what is happening behind the scenes, empowering stakeholders to make informed choices.
explanation.why: Open source and no oversight are different concepts. Jokes are unrelated.

questions.question: Which statement about generative AI models is most accurate?

options.text: They only work with structured data
They generate new content based on patterns learned from training, not from genuine understanding
They are conscious and can reason independently
They always produce factually correct output

explanation.correct: Generative AI generates content based on statistical patterns from training data. It is a probability engine, not a reasoning or conscious entity.
explanation.why: A is wrong — GenAI handles unstructured data well. C is false — AI has no consciousness. D is false — hallucination is a real risk.

questions.question: Why is racial bias in AI healthcare algorithms particularly dangerous?

options.text: It makes the model slower
It costs more to run the model
Patients may not receive appropriate care recommendations, causing real harm
It violates cloud computing SLAs

explanation.correct: When AI systems demonstrate racial bias in healthcare, patients from underrepresented groups may not receive the care they need — a direct, serious harm.
explanation.why: A, B, D are minor concerns compared to the life-affecting consequences of biased medical recommendations.

questions.question: What is the key difference between ML inference and ML training?

options.text: Inference creates the model; training uses the model
Training builds and tunes the model using data; inference applies the trained model to new inputs
Both are identical processes
Inference requires more data than training

explanation.correct: Training is the process of building the model using existing data. Inference is applying the already-trained model to new, unseen inputs to produce output.
explanation.why: A reverses the definitions. C is incorrect — they are distinct phases. D is backward.

questions.question: Which of the following is a valid use case for an LLM?

options.text: Predicting stock prices from structured financial data
Controlling physical robot actuators
Generating code from a natural language description
Sorting a database table by date

explanation.correct: LLMs excel at language tasks including code generation — converting natural language instructions into working code is a primary LLM capability.
explanation.why: A uses structured ML, B is robotics/control systems, D is a simple database operation.

questions.question: What does Amazon Bedrock provide in the AWS AI/ML stack?

options.text: Raw compute like EC2
A middle layer that abstracts infrastructure while giving choice of models
A software-as-a-service email product
A visual IDE for training custom models from scratch

explanation.correct: Bedrock sits in the middle of the AWS AI stack — it abstracts infrastructure complexity while allowing developers to choose from multiple foundation models.
explanation.why: A describes SageMaker infrastructure level. C was WorkMail (deprecated). D is SageMaker Canvas.

questions.question: What is Amazon PartyRock?

options.text: An EC2 instance type optimized for AI
A free playground built on Bedrock where you can build AI apps without managing infrastructure
A music streaming service from AWS
A security auditing tool

explanation.correct: PartyRock is built on Bedrock and provides a free, beginner-friendly playground for experimenting with AI models and building simple AI applications.
explanation.why: A, C, D are all incorrect.

questions.question: Which AWS tool sits at the BOTTOM (infrastructure layer) of the AWS AI/ML stack?

options.text: Amazon Q / Amazon Quick
Amazon Bedrock
Amazon SageMaker
PartyRock

explanation.correct: SageMaker is at the infrastructure layer — analogous to IaaS. It gives full control over compute, datasets, and model training pipelines.
explanation.why: Q/Quick is at the top (SaaS-like). Bedrock is in the middle. PartyRock is at the application layer.

questions.question: What is 'overfitting' in the context of ML model training?

options.text: The model is too small to run on available hardware
The model memorizes training data so well that it fails to generalize to new, unseen data
The model takes too long to train
The model generates output that is too verbose

explanation.correct: Overfitting occurs when a model learns the training data too precisely — including its noise and quirks — and cannot generalize correctly to new examples.
explanation.why: Hardware limits are a different issue. Training time is about compute, not generalization. Verbosity is a generation parameter issue.

questions.question: Why do AI models sometimes fail when input data format changes slightly (e.g., a PNG with a transparency alpha channel)?

options.text: The model charges extra for unusual file formats
The model was not trained on examples containing that specific format variant, so it cannot handle it
AWS throttles unusual file types
Transparency data violates GDPR

explanation.correct: Models are only as capable as their training data. If a specific input variant (like a PNG with an alpha channel) was never in the training set, the model has no learned behavior for it and fails.
explanation.why: A, C, D are all incorrect explanations for this behavior.

questions.question: What is the correct analogy for what happens when you prompt a pre-trained generative AI model?

options.text: You are retraining the model from scratch
You are adding new facts to the model's permanent memory
You are providing new input to a 'preheated oven' — a model already trained — and receiving an inference
You are running a SQL query against a database

explanation.correct: Prompting a pre-trained model is like using a preheated oven — the training (heating) is already done. Your prompt is the new input, and inference is the output.
explanation.why: A and B describe training operations, not inference. D describes structured data querying.

questions.question: What does the AWS Boto3 library do?

options.text: It is a visual dashboard for SageMaker
It is the AWS Python SDK that abstracts AWS API calls into Python code
It is a model training algorithm
It is a firewall for AI endpoints

explanation.correct: Boto3 is the AWS SDK for Python. It allows developers to interact with AWS services (including SageMaker endpoints) through Python code rather than raw API calls.
explanation.why: A describes SageMaker Studio. C describes training algorithms. D is unrelated.

questions.question: A company wants to use AI to classify customer support tickets. Their dataset has 500 examples, the categories change monthly, and they have no ML team. What is the best recommendation?

options.text: Build a custom LLM from scratch
Use SageMaker to train a custom deep learning model
Evaluate whether traditional rule-based classification or a pre-trained Bedrock model is more appropriate first
Use Amazon Quick to write the classification code automatically

explanation.correct: With only 500 examples, no ML team, and changing categories, the first step is evaluating whether ML is even the right approach. A pre-trained Bedrock model with prompting may be far cheaper and faster than custom training.
explanation.why: A requires massive compute and data. B requires ML expertise they don't have. D is an agentic tool, not a classifier.

questions.question: Why is transparency in AI systems important from a regulatory and ethical standpoint?

options.text: It makes the model faster
It allows stakeholders to audit decisions, detect bias, and ensure the system behaves as intended
It reduces the size of the model
It eliminates the need for training data

explanation.correct: Transparency allows stakeholders — including regulators, users, and developers — to validate behavior, detect bias, and make informed choices about AI interactions.
explanation.why: A, C, D are unrelated to transparency as an ethical/governance principle.

questions.question: Which of the following tasks is BEST suited for traditional ML rather than generative AI?

options.text: Writing a blog post about cloud computing
Classifying an image as pizza or not pizza with a binary label
Generating a business proposal
Answering customer FAQs in a chatbot

explanation.correct: Binary image classification is a classical supervised ML task. It does not require generative AI — a trained classifier is simpler, cheaper, and more reliable.
explanation.why: A, C, D all require generating natural language — ideal for LLMs.

questions.question: What is the AWS AI/ML stack layer analogy to 'Platform as a Service' (PaaS)?

options.text: SageMaker (model training infrastructure)
Amazon Bedrock (model access with infrastructure abstracted)
Amazon Q / PartyRock (end-user AI applications)
EC2 (raw compute)

explanation.correct: Bedrock is analogous to PaaS — it abstracts the underlying compute and model training complexity while giving developers controlled access to powerful models.
explanation.why: SageMaker is IaaS-like (full control). Q/PartyRock is SaaS-like. EC2 is raw infrastructure.

questions.question: What characteristic makes AI data labeling work ethically problematic in many current pipelines?

options.text: It requires expensive GPUs
It is often performed by workers in poor conditions for low pay, sometimes reviewing harmful content
It is fully automated
It violates intellectual property law in all jurisdictions

explanation.correct: Much AI training data labeling is done by human workers who are often poorly compensated and sometimes exposed to harmful or traumatic content during content moderation.
explanation.why: A is a hardware concern. C is false — human labelers are critical. D overstates the legal situation.

questions.question: A developer builds an app using an AI coding agent and deploys it without reviewing the generated code. The app causes a DDoS-like pattern and gets shut down by security systems. What is the root lesson?

options.text: AI coding agents should never be used in production
Understanding what the generated code does is essential — AI tools require human review and oversight
AWS security systems are too aggressive
The developer should have used a different programming language

explanation.correct: The root lesson is that even good AI-generated code must be reviewed. Practitioners need to understand the code's behavior, its security implications, and how it appears to external systems.
explanation.why: A is too extreme — agents are valuable tools. C and D miss the core responsibility lesson.

questions.question: What does 'pseudo-intelligence' mean as a term for AI, compared to 'artificial intelligence'?

options.text: It means the AI is broken
It implies the system appears intelligent through pattern matching but does not actually possess intelligence or consciousness
It is a legal term for unlicensed AI
It refers only to older AI systems from the 1980s

explanation.correct: Pseudo-intelligence captures that these systems produce outputs that look intelligent — because they follow human patterns — but they are not conscious, do not reason, and do not actually understand anything.
explanation.why: A, C, D are all incorrect uses of the term.

questions.question: Why can AI facial recognition systems be particularly dangerous when trained on biased datasets?

options.text: They consume too much bandwidth
They may incorrectly identify individuals from underrepresented groups, potentially leading to false accusations or other serious harms
They are too expensive for small companies
They require special GPU hardware

explanation.correct: Facial recognition trained predominantly on certain demographics can fail on others — leading to misidentifications that can result in wrongful accusations and systemic harms.
explanation.why: A, C, D are not the core danger of biased facial recognition systems.
